name: Mint

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Mint likes rich, moist soil and, unlike most kitchen herbs, it loves damp ground. Give it soil with some compost worked in and keep it evenly moist; it will even grow in part shade and in a low, wet spot where other herbs sulk. What it does not like is dry, sandy ground that dries out fast. Because mint spreads so fast underground, most gardeners plant it in a pot or a buried barrier so it cannot take over the bed.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Mint grows in most soils but does best in rich, moist to even damp ground high in organic matter, the opposite of the sharp-drained, lean sites the Mediterranean herbs want. Clemson notes mints prefer rich, moist or even damp soil in part shade, and NC State lists it as unsuited to dry soils, tolerating clay, loam, or sand and both occasionally wet and occasionally dry conditions. Utah State recommends rich, moist, slightly acidic soil with no more than about 1 inch of well-composted organic matter per 100 square feet; do not overfeed, since rich soil and heavy nitrogen make the growth floppy and dilute the flavor. Keep the bed evenly moist but not permanently saturated, and remember mint runs by rhizomes and stolons, so grow it in a sunken bottomless container or a lined bed to keep it in bounds.

ph.note_beginner: Mint grows best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, about 6.0 to 7.0, and it is not fussy. Most garden soil is fine; a simple soil test tells you where you stand.
ph.note_seasoned: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. Utah State describes mint as preferring slightly acidic soil, NC State lists it as tolerant across roughly 6.0 to 8.0, and the University of Minnesota's general herb guidance is a well-drained soil near 6.0 to 7.5, so mint is forgiving and rarely needs any pH adjustment beyond a soil-test baseline.

fertilizer.timing: a light feeding in early spring as growth resumes, with a second light feeding midseason only if the patch looks pale
fertilizer.example_product: 16-16-16 or a balanced all-purpose fertilizer, or a topdressing of compost
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Mint is a light feeder and is easily overfed. Utah State suggests about one teaspoon of a balanced 16-16-16 fertilizer per plant in early spring as growth resumes; a compost-rich bed often needs no more than a light topdressing. Go easy, because rich soil and heavy nitrogen push soft, floppy stems and thin the essential oils that carry mint's flavor and aroma, a point Wisconsin Horticulture makes for mints grown in lean ground. In a container, where frequent watering leaches nutrients, a dilute liquid feed every few weeks through the growing season keeps the leaves green.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Mint does not need much feeding, and too much makes it flop and lose flavor. Mix a little compost or balanced fertilizer into the soil in spring, then leave it alone. If you grow it in a pot, feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to give your mint a light spring feeding as it regrows.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Time to give your mint a light feeding.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A light, balanced feed is all mint wants: about a teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring, or a compost topdressing. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which makes the stems floppy and waters down the flavor.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer such as 16-16-16, just a light feeding in spring. Do not overdo it; too much makes mint floppy and bland.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: About one teaspoon of 16-16-16 per plant in early spring (Utah State); a compost-rich or container bed often needs only a light topdressing or a dilute liquid feed every 3 to 4 weeks.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A teaspoon of balanced fertilizer per plant in spring, or a thin layer of compost; in a pot, a diluted liquid feed every few weeks.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_beginner: Clusters of tiny soft green or gray insects on the growing tips and undersides of leaves, sometimes with curled, sticky foliage.
pests.cause_beginner: Aphids are small sap-sucking insects that breed fast, especially on soft growth from too much fertilizer, and they can spread plant viruses.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water, or use insecticidal soap or neem oil on the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Rinse cut sprigs well before use.
pests.prevention_beginner: Welcome ladybugs and lacewings, go easy on nitrogen, and check new growth often.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Colonies on growing tips and leaf undersides, one of the pests UC IPM lists for mint; honeydew and the insects themselves contaminate a crop eaten fresh, and soft, overfed growth is the most susceptible.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several aphid species feed on mint; they reproduce rapidly and favor the lush growth that excess nitrogen and rich soil produce.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dislodge colonies with a water jet or spray insecticidal soap or neem, covering leaf undersides, and repeat every few days; conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitoid wasps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout the tips early, avoid overfeeding, and conserve natural enemies; because you eat the leaves, lean toward a strong water spray before anything else.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_beginner: A fine stippling or speckling on the leaves, sometimes with faint webbing on the undersides, worst in hot, dry weather. Leaves look dull, sandy, or bronzed.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking mites, not true insects, that explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions and are easy to miss until the leaves are speckled.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with a strong jet of water to knock them off, keep the plant well watered, and use insecticidal soap or neem if they persist.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched, since drought stress invites mites, and rinse dusty foliage in hot spells.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Twospotted and related spider mites, which UC IPM lists for mint, stipple the foliage with pale flecks and spin fine webbing on the undersides; they flare in hot, dry, dusty conditions and on drought-stressed plants, which is why mint's moisture love is also its best mite defense.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spider mites feeding with piercing mouthparts; populations build fastest in heat and drought and on dusty, water-stressed plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hose the undersides forcefully and repeat, maintain steady soil moisture, and apply insecticidal soap or a miticidal oil to the leaf undersides; conserve predatory mites and minute pirate bugs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not let mint dry out or get dusty, mulch to hold moisture, and scout the undersides in hot weather when mites move fastest.

pests.name: Cutworms, mint flea beetles, and root-feeding pests
pests.symptoms_beginner: Young shoots cut off at the soil line, notched or shot-holed leaves, or plants that weaken and thin out from grubs feeding on the roots and rhizomes.
pests.cause_beginner: A mix of chewing pests, cutworms and mint flea beetles above ground and root-feeding larvae below, that damage leaves, stems, and the underground runners.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Handpick cutworms at dusk and use cardboard collars on new transplants, hose or handpick flea beetles, and keep the bed clean; dividing and resetting a tired patch in fresh ground breaks root-pest cycles.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clear plant debris where cutworms shelter, rotate a heavily infested patch to fresh ground, and keep plants vigorous so they outgrow light feeding.
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Utah State lists flea beetles and cutworms among mint's insect pests; cutworms sever young shoots at the soil line and mint flea beetles chew small holes, while soil and rhizome feeders thin an established patch from below. On a home planting numbers are usually modest.
pests.cause_seasoned: A complex of foliage feeders (cutworms, mint flea beetle) and root/rhizome feeders (root and rhizome larvae); the perennial, spreading root mass is what harbors the below-ground stages.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Handpick and use collars against cutworms, dislodge flea beetles with water or row cover on new plantings, and manage root pests culturally by dividing and resetting the patch in clean soil; reserve any spray for the labeled edible-herb products.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Sanitize debris, keep plants vigorous, and reset an infested patch into fresh ground on a multi-year cycle, the same renewal that keeps mint from getting woody.

diseases.name: Mint rust
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Small orange, yellow, or rust-brown powdery pustules on the undersides of the leaves and on the stems, with pale spots on the upper surface. Badly affected leaves curl, brown, and drop, and rusty leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: A rust fungus, the signature mint disease, that thrives in warm, humid, crowded conditions and lives over on the roots and rhizomes from year to year.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick off and destroy rusted leaves as soon as you see them, thin and space plants for airflow, water at the soil line, and cut a badly infected patch to the ground; in a severe case, start a fresh planting from clean, rust-free cuttings in a new spot.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space plants for good airflow, avoid wetting the foliage, keep the patch from getting congested, and start new plantings from clean stock.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Puccinia menthae, the classic mint rust: orange to brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides, stems, and petioles, with defoliation in a bad year (NC State lists rust among the main mint diseases). It overwinters in the rhizomes, so an infected patch reinfects itself, and warm humid crowding drives it.
diseases.cause_seasoned: The rust fungus Puccinia menthae, favored by warm, humid, crowded conditions and carried over in the root and rhizome mass.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infected leaves, open up the planting for airflow, switch to soil-line watering, and mow or cut a heavily infected patch to the ground and clear the debris; renew from clean cuttings in fresh ground where it recurs. There is no reliable home cure once it is established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Airflow, dry foliage, and uncongested spacing are the defenses; propagate only from rust-free plants and reset a chronically infected patch elsewhere.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Stunted, off-color plants whose lower leaves yellow and wilt, often on just one side of a stem, with whole shoots or plants dying back in warm weather. It does not wash off and there is no spray cure.
diseases.cause_beginner: A soil-borne fungus that clogs the plant's water-conducting tissue; it builds up in the ground and is the disease that shortens the life of a mint patch.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure for an infected plant, so remove it. Start fresh plantings from clean cuttings in a new bed, and do not follow tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries, which host the same fungus.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant clean stock in ground with no recent history of the disease, avoid siting mint after verticillium-susceptible crops, and move the patch to fresh ground every few years.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Verticillium wilt (a soilborne Verticillium), the disease that most limits mint's longevity: slow, bronze-cast spring growth, one-sided branch development, lower-leaf yellowing and wilt in warm or dry weather, and dieback. The Connecticut Experiment Station and Utah State both flag it for mint. The fungus persists in soil for years and has a wide host range, so it is managed by site selection and renewal, not treatment.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A soilborne Verticillium fungus that invades the vascular system; it survives for years in soil and infects many crops (tomato, potato, strawberry, other mints).
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rogue out affected plants and manage by prevention: propagate disease-free cuttings, establish new patches in clean ground away from prior verticillium hosts, and rotate the mint bed on a multi-year cycle where the disease appears.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean stock, avoid ground that grew tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, or strawberries, and reset the patch in fresh soil periodically, since there is no rescue for an infected plant.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew and anthracnose (leaf spot)
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A white, powdery dust on the leaves and stems (powdery mildew), or dark sunken spots and blotches on leaves and stems (anthracnose leaf spot). Heavily spotted or coated leaves are not good to eat.
diseases.cause_beginner: Fungal leaf diseases that spread in crowded, humid plantings and on wet foliage, worse where air does not move.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Remove affected leaves, thin the planting and water at the soil line to keep the leaves dry, and cut a badly hit patch back to encourage clean new growth.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Space for airflow, water at the base rather than overhead, and avoid crowding.
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Powdery mildew (white powdery patches that brown and shrivel heavy foliage, listed for mint by UC IPM) and anthracnose or leaf spot (Utah State and NC State list leaf-spotting fungi for mint), both favored by crowded, humid conditions and wet leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Foliar fungi (powdery mildew; anthracnose and other leaf-spot fungi) driven by high humidity, crowding, and prolonged leaf wetness.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow by thinning and dividing, water at the soil line, remove infected foliage, and shear a badly affected patch to force clean regrowth; drip irrigation and avoiding overnight leaf wetness are the practical controls Utah State recommends.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Open the canopy, keep the foliage dry, and do not let the patch get congested; renew a chronically diseased stand from clean cuttings.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Roughly 1 to 2 inches of water per week, kept even; mint is a moisture lover that must not dry out, and Utah State advises 1 to 2 inches per week while cautioning against overwatering, which invites disease.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water often enough to keep the soil evenly moist, about 1 to 2 inches a week. Mint likes damp soil, so do not let it dry out.
watering.amount_seasoned: About 1 to 2 inches per week, more in heat and in containers, which dry fast; the goal is steady, even moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. Mulch helps hold it.
watering.amount_beginner: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches a week, more when it is hot or in a pot. Keep the soil damp but not swampy.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the soil line with drip or a soaker hose; keeping the foliage dry checks mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot on a crop eaten fresh, which Utah State reinforces with its drip-irrigation and no-overnight-wet-leaves advice.
watering.method_beginner: Water at the base of the plants rather than over the leaves, which helps prevent the leaf diseases mint is prone to.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves and root or crown rot in ground that stays waterlogged, plus more rust and mildew where the foliage stays wet; mint tolerates damp soil but not standing water.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Lower leaves yellow and the plant can rot at the base if the soil stays soggy, and wet leaves bring on leaf diseases.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, dull or bronzed leaves, and a spike in spider mites; sustained drought stress checks growth and, in hot dry regions, scorches the foliage, since mint has little drought tolerance.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, dull leaves and more spider mites when the soil dries out. Mint does not handle drought well, so keep it watered.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, kept even
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new division or cutting roots in; mint is a moisture lover and must not dry out as it establishes. Water at the soil line and mulch to hold even moisture.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep the soil evenly moist while a new mint plant gets rooted. Mint loves damp soil, so do not let it dry out now.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, even and generous
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Mint is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, the opposite of rosemary or thyme: give an even, generous 1 to 2 inches a week (USU's figure), more in heat or in fast-drying containers, aiming for steady moisture rather than a soak-and-dry cycle. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves, against mint rust, powdery mildew, and leaf spot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Mint likes damp soil, unlike most herbs. Keep it evenly and generously watered, about 1 to 2 inches a week and more in heat or in a pot, but never swampy. Water the soil, not the leaves, to avoid the diseases mint gets.

schedule_by_stage.rate: about 1 to 2 inches per week, even and generous
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Keep the same even, generous moisture through the cutting season; mint has little drought tolerance, and a dry spell checks growth, dulls or bronzes the leaves, and can bring on spider mites.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Keep mint evenly and generously watered while you cut it. If it dries out the leaves go dull and bronzed and spider mites move in, so keep the soil damp.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Cut back watering as the patch dies back for winter; a dormant patch needs little, and constantly waterlogged winter ground invites root and crown rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: Water little while mint is dormant over winter. Soggy winter ground can rot the roots, so ease right off.

schedule_by_stage.rate: resume about 1 to 2 inches per week
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: As shoots push up in spring, resume even, generous watering to drive the tender new growth; an established patch is tougher but still resents drought.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: As new shoots come up in spring, start watering evenly again to push tender new growth.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Even, generous moisture is the whole trick with mint: it is the rare kitchen herb that thrives in damp ground and part shade, so treat it the opposite of rosemary or thyme. The one caution is disease, so water the soil, not the leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Keep mint's soil steadily moist; it loves damp ground, unlike most herbs. Just water the soil and not the leaves to avoid disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: Steady moisture matters most while a new division or cutting is rooting in and through hot, dry spells; an established patch is tougher but still resents drought.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: Keep the soil moist while new plants are getting established and during hot, dry weather.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start mint from a division, a rooted cutting, or a nursery transplant, not from seed: named mints such as peppermint are hybrids and, as Clemson notes, mint seed does not come true to type, so seedlings are variable. Divide and reset established clumps in early spring (Utah State, Minnesota), or root stem or stolon cuttings in water or moist mix at almost any time in the growing season (Wisconsin, Maryland). Set plants out around the last spring frost; mint is very hardy, so timing is forgiving. Whatever you plant, put it in a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed, because mint spreads aggressively by runners. If you do start from seed, surface-sow it because the seed needs light to germinate, keep it around 60 to 70°F, and start indoors 6 to 8 weeks before setting out; expect the variable, off-type seedlings noted above.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easy way to start mint is from a small plant, a cutting, or a piece dug from a friend's patch, not from seed (seed-grown mint is a gamble and often tastes of nothing in particular). If you do want to try seed anyway, press the tiny seed onto the surface and do not cover it, since it needs light to sprout, and start it indoors about 6 to 8 weeks before your last frost. Just root a sprig in a glass of water or plant a division in spring. Because mint spreads fast, plant it in a pot or a buried, bottomless container so it cannot run through your whole garden.

drainage.saucer_practice: Empty the saucer after watering so the roots stay moist but never sit in standing water, which invites rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: A good-quality potting mix, not garden soil.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost so it holds moisture and stays a little rich.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: A moisture-retentive potting mix with plenty of organic matter, since mint likes to stay damp.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in compost for water-holding and a little balanced starter fertilizer; do not overdo the nitrogen or the plant flops.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out fast and mint hates drying out, so check daily in warm weather and keep the mix evenly moist.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed lightly with a diluted liquid fertilizer every few weeks, since watering washes nutrients out of pots.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Mint is very hardy and comes back every spring, but a pot freezes harder than the open ground because the roots are exposed on all sides. In cold areas, sink the pot in the ground for winter, move it against the house or into an unheated shed, or mulch over it. Cut the top back after frost; it will resprout from the roots in spring.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Mint is a hardy herbaceous perennial (Utah State rates it hardy to about -20°F), so a container overwinters readily, but the confined root ball is more exposed to freezing than in-ground crowns. In cold zones sink the pot, move it to a cold frame or unheated structure, or heap mulch over it; the top dies back and regrows from the roots and rhizomes in spring. This is also the moment to lift, divide, and refresh a potbound clump.

container_notes.notes_beginner: A pot is the best way to grow mint, because it keeps the roots from running all over the garden. Use a container at least 8 inches deep, keep it watered, and snip sprigs often. It is happy on a partly shaded step or windowsill and comes back year after year.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers are the standard way to grow mint, because they cage the aggressive rhizomes that otherwise colonize a bed; Maryland, UF/IFAS, and Wisconsin all recommend potting mint or using a bottomless sunken container to confine it. Use a pot at least 8 inches deep and keep the mix steadily moist, since pots dry fast and mint has little drought tolerance. Divide and repot every year or two when the clump crowds itself, and cut back after frost for a clean flush in spring.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry faster than beds and mint will not tolerate drying out, so check daily in warmth and water before the mix dries.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Container mint needs a light but regular feed, a dilute liquid fertilizer every 3 to 4 weeks, because frequent watering leaches the limited mix; keep nitrogen modest to preserve flavor.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering container suits mint well, since it smooths out the steady moisture the plant wants and reduces the drought stress that brings on spider mites.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot is a good match because it keeps mint's soil evenly damp, which is exactly what it likes.
container_notes.shape_requirements_seasoned: Depth matters less than confinement: a pot 8 inches or deeper holds enough moisture, but the real job of the container is to wall off the running rhizomes, so choose a solid-sided pot rather than a fabric bag if you plan to sink it in a bed.
container_notes.shape_requirements_beginner: Use a pot at least 8 inches deep with solid sides. The main point of the pot is to stop the roots from spreading, so a solid container works better than a cloth bag if you bury it in the garden.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid establishing a new mint patch where tomatoes, potatoes, eggplant, peppers, or strawberries recently grew: those crops host Verticillium, the soilborne wilt that most limits mint's longevity. Following one mint patch immediately with another in the same ground also concentrates mint rust and verticillium, which carry over in soil and rhizomes.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant mint where tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries just grew, because they share a soil disease (verticillium wilt) that also attacks mint.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (peas, beans), brassicas (cabbage family), alliums (onion, garlic), or corn, none of which build up mint's diseases.
rotation.note_seasoned: Mint is a permanent perennial planting rather than a rotated annual, so rotation here is mostly about where you establish or renew a patch. Because verticillium wilt and mint rust persist in soil and rhizomes, site a new planting in clean ground with no recent history of Verticillium hosts (tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper, strawberry) or of a diseased mint stand, and plan to reset the patch in fresh soil every few years if disease or root pests build up. Utah State and commercial mint guidance both treat multi-year renewal as the core disease defense.
rotation.note_beginner: You plant mint once and it stays for years, so there is no yearly rotation. Just start it in clean ground that did not just grow tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries, and if a patch gets diseased, start fresh plants in a new spot.

bolting.triggers: flowering in mid to late summer
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Mint does not bolt the way a cool-season annual does; as a perennial it simply sends up flower spikes in mid to late summer. Flowering is not a disaster, the bees love it, but once mint blooms the leaves turn a little tougher and less aromatic and the plant puts energy into seed. To keep tender, flavorful leaves, pinch or shear off the flower buds as they form and harvest regularly, which Clemson notes is exactly how frequent cutting keeps mint from flowering. A hard shear to a few inches after a bloom flush brings a clean new crop of leaves.
bolting.prevention_beginner: Mint is not like cilantro; it will not bolt and quit in the heat. It just tries to flower in mid to late summer. The flowers are fine for bees, but the leaves get a bit tougher, so pinch off the flower buds and keep cutting the plant to keep the best leaves coming.
bolting.note_seasoned: The flower spikes are a normal part of a perennial mint's year, not a failure. Left to bloom, mint feeds pollinators and can self-sow (seedlings come untrue and may be weak), and the foliage coarsens; sheared before or during bloom, the plant resets into fresh leafy growth. Many growers let part of a patch flower for the pollinators and keep another part cut for the kitchen.
bolting.note_beginner: Mint flowering in summer is normal. If you want the best leaves, snip the flower buds off and cut the plant back now and then. If you would rather feed the bees, let some of it bloom; it will not hurt the plant.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fresh-cut mint wilts within a day at room temperature, so refrigerate promptly; standing the cut stems in a glass of water on the counter holds them a few days, like cut flowers.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Do not leave cut mint out on the counter, where it wilts. Chill it, or stand the stems in a glass of water like a little bouquet.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate fresh mint unwashed in a loose or perforated bag, or with the stems in a little water under a loose bag, in the crisper; it holds about a week. Wash only at use, since trapped moisture speeds breakdown and blackening.
storage.fridge_beginner: Store fresh mint unwashed in a loose bag in the fridge, where it keeps about a week. Wash it only when you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Mint freezes well chopped into ice-cube trays with water for drinks and cooking, or blended into sauces; frozen sprigs lose their crispness for garnish but keep their flavor. It also dries, but as UF/IFAS warns, dry it in darkness and low humidity or the leaves turn dark and moldy.
storage.freezer_beginner: Freeze chopped mint in an ice-cube tray with a little water for drinks and cooking. You can also dry it, but dry it somewhere dark and dry or the leaves go dark and moldy.
storage.notes_seasoned: Because a mint patch keeps producing, the easiest storage is to cut sprigs as needed. Cut mint keeps about a week refrigerated. For longer keeping, freeze it (chopped in cubes or in sauces) or dry it; Maryland notes leaves for drying are best cut just as the flowers begin to open, when the oils peak, and UF/IFAS stresses drying in darkness and low humidity to keep the color and avoid mold.
storage.notes_beginner: The best way to store mint is to leave it growing and cut what you need. Picked mint keeps about a week in the fridge. To save extra, freeze it in ice-cube trays or dry it in a dark, dry spot.

recommended.name: Spearmint (Mentha spicata)
recommended.note: The classic culinary mint, mild and sweet; the traditional choice for tea, mint juleps, tabbouleh, and lamb. One of the easiest and hardiest mints. Propagate from cuttings or division.

recommended.name: Peppermint (Mentha x piperita)
recommended.note: Stronger, cooler, and more menthol-forward than spearmint, with a candy-cane note; a natural hybrid of water mint and spearmint. Being a hybrid, it does not come true from seed, so grow it from cuttings or divisions.

recommended.name: Chocolate mint
recommended.note: A peppermint selection with a dark stem and a cocoa-and-mint aroma; popular for desserts and drinks. Grown from cuttings or division.

recommended.name: Apple or woolly mint (Mentha suaveolens)
recommended.note: Soft, fuzzy, round leaves with a fruity, mild apple-mint flavor; the variegated pineapple mint is a form of it. Tolerates some shade and is a bit less aggressive than spearmint.

recommended.name: Mojito mint (Mentha x villosa)
recommended.note: The traditional Cuban mint for mojitos, milder and less biting than peppermint, with a warm, almost bubblegum note. Grown from cuttings.

recommended.name: Orange or bergamot mint (Mentha x piperita citrata)
recommended.note: A citrus-scented peppermint form used in teas, fruit dishes, and drinks. Like other named mints it is propagated vegetatively, not from seed.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose mint by flavor, since culture is nearly identical across the genus. Spearmint (Mentha spicata) is the mild, sweet all-purpose culinary mint and among the hardiest; peppermint (Mentha x piperita) is the stronger, cooler, menthol type and, as a hybrid, must be grown from cuttings or division rather than seed. Flavored selections such as chocolate, orange or bergamot, apple or woolly (and its variegated pineapple mint form), and mojito mint (Mentha x villosa) all grow the same way. Because named mints are hybrids or selections, Clemson notes mint seed does not come true to type, so propagate every one of these from cuttings, divisions, or transplants. Keep different mints apart if you want to preserve distinct flavors, and contain every one of them.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick mint by how it tastes, since they all grow the same. Spearmint is the mild, sweet everyday mint and the easiest; peppermint is stronger and cooler. There are fun flavored kinds too, like chocolate, apple, orange, and mojito mint. Grow any of them from a cutting or a division, not from seed, because seed-grown mint is unpredictable. And whatever you pick, give it a pot so it does not take over.

companions.note_beginner: Mint has a real gift and a real hazard as a companion. Its strong scent is said to confuse pests like cabbage moths, aphids, and flea beetles, and when it flowers it draws in bees and helpful insects. The hazard is that mint spreads so aggressively it will smother its neighbors, so the golden rule is to grow it in a pot, even when it is near the plants it helps. Keep it away from chamomile and other quiet herbs it would overrun, and away from your other mints so the flavors stay distinct.
companions.note_seasoned: Mint's companion value is mostly aromatic and pollinator-based: its volatile oils are traditionally credited with deterring cabbage moths, aphids, ants, and flea beetles, and a flowering patch is a strong nectar source for bees and predatory insects. The overriding practical fact, though, is its aggression, so any interplanting benefit is realized by sinking mint in a container next to the crop rather than letting it loose in the bed. The well-grounded cautions are structural: keep mint out of the open ground near less vigorous herbs (chamomile, and slower perennials) that it will overrun, and keep different mints separated to preserve their distinct flavors and to slow shared rust.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Mint's strong smell is traditionally said to put off the cabbage moths and flea beetles that attack cabbage-family plants. Grow the mint in a sunken pot nearby so it helps without taking over.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic pest-confusion of brassica pests by mint is a widespread companion tradition with a plausible volatile-oil mechanism, but not measured in a mint-specific trial.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional aromatic pairing: mint's essential oils are long credited with masking or deterring cabbage moths and flea beetles on brassicas. Sound by mechanism and tradition rather than a measured trial, and only safe if the mint is contained.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Mint is often planted near tomatoes and peppers to help repel aphids and other pests with its scent, and its flowers bring in helpful insects. Keep it in a pot so its roots do not invade.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: A common companion tradition (aromatic pest deterrence plus beneficial attraction); no mint-tomato trial found, and note tomatoes share verticillium with mint, so keep the mint contained and off that ground.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A traditional aromatic and beneficial-insect pairing; the caution is that tomatoes, peppers, and mint share Verticillium, so a contained mint next to them must not later be planted into that soil.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Pollinators and beneficial insects (when flowering)
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: If you let some mint bloom, the flowers feed bees, hoverflies, and other good bugs that also eat garden pests. Let one contained clump flower for them.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Flowering mint as a nectar/insectary source is well supported by observation and general extension guidance on flowering herbs; the pest-suppression benefit follows the standard insectary mechanism.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: A genuine insectary function: a flowering mint patch recruits bees and aphid-eating hoverflies and parasitoids, the same mechanism extension services cite for flowering herbs. Realized best by letting one contained clump bloom while others stay cut.

good_seasoned.name: Brassicas (cabbage, broccoli, kale)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Mint's volatile oils are traditionally credited with deterring cabbage moths and flea beetles on brassicas; a mechanism-and-tradition pairing, safe only when the mint is contained.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Widespread aromatic-deterrence tradition, plausible mechanism, no mint-specific trial.

good_seasoned.name: Tomatoes and peppers
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Traditionally interplanted for aromatic pest deterrence and, in bloom, beneficial-insect attraction; keep the mint contained and remember it shares Verticillium with these crops.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Common companion tradition; unmeasured on mint, and a shared-verticillium caution applies.

good_seasoned.name: Pollinators and beneficial insects (when flowering)
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A flowering mint patch is a real insectary, drawing bees and aphid-eating hoverflies and parasitoids, the standard flowering-herb mechanism. Let one contained clump bloom while others stay cut for the kitchen.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: Flowering herbs as insectary plants are well supported; the specific pest-suppression benefit follows the same mechanism.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Other mints and quiet herbs (chamomile, marjoram)
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Do not plant mint loose in a bed next to gentler herbs like chamomile or marjoram, because mint will run over them. And keep different mints apart, or their flavors blur together and they trade diseases.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Mint's aggressive rhizomatous spread and the recommendation to contain it are documented by Clemson, NC State, UMD, UF/IFAS, USU, and Wisconsin; crowding also spreads mint rust.

bad_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: The signature caution: mint's rhizomes overrun less vigorous neighbors, so keep it out of open ground beside chamomile, marjoram, and slower perennials. Separate different mints to preserve distinct flavors and to slow the rust that congestion spreads. Extension-supported (contain mint) rather than folklore.

bad_seasoned.name: Other mints and quiet herbs (chamomile, marjoram)
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Mint's running rhizomes smother gentler herbs, so keep it contained and out of shared open ground; separate different mints to preserve flavor and slow rust. Extension-supported, since every mint source recommends confining the plant.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Contain-the-mint is universal extension guidance (Clemson, NC State, UMD, UF/IFAS, USU, Wisconsin); congestion also spreads rust.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A newly set division, cutting, or transplant putting out fresh roots and the first new shoots. Early growth is upright before the plant begins to run.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Your new mint plant starting to root in and push new leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep the soil evenly moist while roots take hold, and make sure the plant is in its container or barrier before it starts to spread.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water regularly so it does not dry out, and get it into a pot or a buried barrier now, before it runs.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is the new mint rooting in?

growth_stages.name: Vegetative spread
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fast leafy growth as the plant sends out runners (stolons and rhizomes) and fills its space; this is when containment earns its keep.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Lots of new leafy stems and runners spreading out.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep it watered and, in part shade or hot regions, watch for scorch; pinch tips to encourage bushy growth and check that runners are not escaping the container.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep it moist, pinch the tips to make it bushy, and watch that it does not creep out of its pot.

growth_stages.name: Harvest (cut-and-come-again)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full, leafy stems you cut from repeatedly; take sprigs or shear the patch and it flushes back within a couple of weeks all season.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Full, leafy plants you can keep cutting from.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back, never more than about a third at a time, or shear the whole patch to a few inches to force a clean flush; pinch flower buds to keep the leaves tender. Utah State harvests two to three times a season, cutting to within about an inch of the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Snip sprigs as you need them, or cut the whole patch back by a third and it grows again. Pinch off flower buds to keep the leaves nice.

growth_stages.name: Dormancy (dieback and overwinter)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: In cold zones the top growth yellows and dies back after frost while the roots and rhizomes overwinter; in frost-free zones the plant stays evergreen but slows.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In cold areas the tops die back for winter; the roots stay alive underground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut the dead top growth back to the ground after a hard frost and mulch cold-zone or container plantings; the crown and rhizomes survive to about -20°F. Do not dig it up, it is not dead.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: After frost, cut the dead tops off and add a little mulch in cold areas. The plant is not dead; it will come back in spring.

growth_stages.name: Spring regrowth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New shoots rising from the overwintered crown and rhizomes as the soil warms, the yearly restart of a perennial you planted once.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Fresh new shoots coming up from the roots in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: This is the moment to lift and divide a crowded clump, refresh the soil with a little compost, and give a light spring feeding; thin escaping runners now while they are easy to pull.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: When new shoots appear, you can dig and split a crowded clump, add a little compost, and pull any runners that have escaped.

notifications.title_beginner: Get your mint in a pot
notifications.body_seasoned: Your mint is establishing. Make sure it is in a container or a buried, bottomless barrier now, before the runners spread into the bed and become hard to remove.
notifications.body_beginner: Your mint is settling in. Put it in a pot or a buried barrier now so it does not take over the garden.

notifications.body_seasoned: Your mint is full enough to harvest. Cut stems back by no more than a third, or shear the patch to a few inches, and it regrows within a couple of weeks. Pinch off flower buds to keep the leaves tender.
notifications.body_beginner: Your mint is big enough to pick. Snip sprigs or cut it back by a third and it grows again. Pinch off any flower buds.

notifications.body_seasoned: As new shoots rise in spring, lift and divide a crowded clump, refresh the soil, and give a light feeding. This is also the time to pull any runners that escaped the container over the season.
notifications.body_beginner: When mint comes back in spring, you can dig it up and split it, add compost, and feed it lightly. Pull out any runners that got loose.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Mint is a moisture lover with little drought tolerance, so a hot, dry spell scorches the foliage and invites spider mites, and in arid and desert regions the leaves can burn outright. Keep the soil evenly moist, mulch the roots, give afternoon shade where summers are fierce, and harvest in the cool morning; in the low desert and hot interior the planting calendar pauses through the worst heat.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Mint does not like hot, dry weather and can scorch or get spider mites. Water it well, mulch it, and give it afternoon shade where summers are brutal. In the hottest desert areas it takes a summer break until things cool down.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Mint is a very hardy perennial, hardy to roughly -20°F, so a freeze that kills the top growth does not kill the plant. Let the tops die back, cut them off, and mulch cold-zone or container roots; the crown and rhizomes overwinter and resprout in spring. No rescue is needed for the foliage.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Mint is very hardy, so a freeze that browns the leaves will not kill it. Let the tops die back, trim them off, and add a little mulch in cold spots. It will come back from the roots in spring.

establishment.text_seasoned: Start mint from a division, a rooted cutting, or a transplant, not seed (named mints do not come true from seed), and get it into a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed at planting. Containing it on day one is far easier than digging out runners later.
establishment.text_beginner: Plant mint from a cutting or a small plant, not seed, and put it straight into a pot or buried barrier so it cannot spread everywhere.

vegetative.text_seasoned: Mint runs by shallow rhizomes and stolons and can colonize a bed fast. Keep it evenly moist (it has little drought tolerance), pinch the tips for bushiness, and patrol the edges of the container for escaping runners, which pull easily while young.
vegetative.text_beginner: Keep mint watered and pinch the growing tips so it gets bushy. Check the edges of its pot for runners trying to escape and pull them while they are small.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again: take sprigs or cut stems back by up to a third, or shear the whole patch to about an inch above the soil, and it flushes back in a couple of weeks. Utah State cuts two to three times a season. Frequent cutting also keeps mint from flowering and going coarse.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick sprigs whenever you want, or cut the whole plant back by a third and it grows again. Cutting it often keeps the leaves tender and stops it flowering.

dormancy.text_seasoned: In cold zones let frost take the tops, then cut the dead growth to the ground and mulch; the crown and rhizomes are hardy to about -20°F and overwinter fine. Cutting the old foliage back at season's end, as Wisconsin advises, also clears overwintering rust.
dormancy.text_beginner: In cold areas, after frost cut the dead tops off and add a little mulch. The roots survive winter and the plant comes back in spring. Clearing the old leaves also helps prevent disease.

spring_regrowth.text_seasoned: Spring is renewal time: as shoots emerge, lift and divide a crowded clump and replant the vigorous outer pieces in refreshed soil (Utah State and Minnesota both divide in early spring), give a light balanced feeding, and thin any runners that escaped over winter.
spring_regrowth.text_beginner: When mint comes up in spring, dig up a crowded clump and split it, replanting the healthy outer pieces. Feed it lightly and pull any runners that got loose.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A single mint plant becomes a spreading patch within a season and, cut repeatedly, yields far more than a household uses; one or two contained plants supply a kitchen. Yield builds year over year as the clump thickens, which is also why division and renewal matter.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One mint plant quickly becomes a whole patch and gives you more than you can use, so one or two plants are plenty. It comes back bigger each year.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Production runs from late spring through fall in cold zones and nearly year-round in frost-free ones, dipping only in the hottest arid summers and in winter dormancy. Regular shearing keeps the flushes coming and the leaves tender.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: Mint produces from spring through fall, and almost all year in mild climates. Keep cutting it and it keeps coming.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Mint is one of the easiest crops to succeed with in year one, so easy that the beginner mistake is not failing to grow it but failing to contain it. Plant a division or cutting in moist, part-shade ground inside a barrier, keep it watered, cut it often, and it establishes fast and returns every spring for years.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Mint is very easy to grow the first year. The only real mistake is not containing it. Plant it in a pot in moist soil, keep it watered, cut it often, and it comes back every year.
factors_seasoned: Containment: the single biggest decision is a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed, since uncontained mint takes over and becomes hard to remove.

Even moisture and part shade: mint is a moisture lover with little drought tolerance and, unusually for an herb, tolerates and even wants some shade, especially in hot regions where full sun scorches it.
Harvest and shearing: frequent cutting keeps leaves tender, prevents flowering, and forces fresh flushes all season.
Renewal: dividing and resetting the patch every few years in clean ground restores vigor and outruns mint rust, verticillium wilt, and root pests.
Restraint with fertilizer: rich soil and heavy nitrogen make floppy, less flavorful growth, so feed lightly.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No reliable extension or peer-reviewed evidence supports timing mint planting or harvest by moon phase. Plant divisions and cuttings by soil warmth and frost dates, and harvest whenever the plant is full and before it flowers heavily.

failure_diagnostics.label: Mint took over the garden
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Mint spreads fast underground by runners, and once loose it is very hard to remove.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your mint escaped its spot and spread through the bed, popping up among other plants. That is mint being mint: it runs by rhizomes and stolons and, as Utah State puts it, once established it is very hard to eradicate. Next time, plant it in a pot or a bottomless container sunk in the ground, leaving an inch of rim above soil, and pull escaping runners while they are small.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow mint in a pot or a buried, bottomless container, and pull stray runners early.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: The patch colonized the bed through shallow rhizomes and stolons, the defining mint behavior every extension source warns about (contain it in a sunken bottomless container or lined bed). Runners left unpulled root at the nodes and become hard to eradicate. Next time confine at planting and edge the container above the soil line.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Uncontained rhizomatous and stoloniferous spread, mint's signature growth habit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confine at planting in a sunken bottomless container (rim above grade) or a lined bed, and patrol for and pull escaping runners while young.

failure_diagnostics.label: Orange or brown pustules on the leaves
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Mint rust, the classic mint disease, which lives over in the roots and spreads in crowded, humid plantings.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your mint leaves developed orange to rust-brown powdery spots, mostly on the undersides, and some curled and dropped. That is mint rust (Puccinia menthae). It overwinters in the rhizomes, so the patch reinfects itself, and crowding and wet leaves make it worse. Next time, thin and space the plants, water at the soil line, remove rusty leaves, and cut a bad patch to the ground; renew from clean cuttings in a new spot if it keeps coming back.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Space and thin for airflow, water at the base, remove rusty leaves, and renew badly infected patches from clean cuttings.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Orange-brown pustules on leaf undersides, stems, and petioles with defoliation indicate mint rust (Puccinia menthae), favored by crowding, humidity, and leaf wetness and carried over in the rhizomes. Next time open the canopy, switch to soil-line watering, sanitize infected foliage, shear or mow a severe patch, and re-establish from rust-free stock in clean ground.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: The rust fungus Puccinia menthae, overwintering in rhizomes and driven by congestion and wet foliage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin for airflow, irrigate at the soil line, remove infected leaves, cut back a severe patch, and renew from clean cuttings in a new site.

failure_diagnostics.label: Speckled, dull leaves in hot, dry weather
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Spider mites, which explode on drought-stressed mint in heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your mint leaves looked stippled, dull, or bronzed, maybe with fine webbing underneath, during a hot dry spell. Those are spider mites, and they thrive when mint is hot, dusty, and dry, exactly the stress mint hates. Next time, keep the soil evenly moist and mulched, hose off the leaf undersides, and give afternoon shade in fierce heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep mint evenly moist and mulched, rinse the leaf undersides, and shade it in extreme heat.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A fine pale stippling with faint webbing on the undersides in hot, dry weather points to spider mites, which UC IPM lists for mint and which flare on drought-stressed, dusty plants. Next time maintain steady moisture and mulch, wash the undersides forcefully and repeat, conserve predatory mites, and provide afternoon shade in the hottest regions, since mint's moisture love is its best mite defense.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Spider mites, favored by heat, dust, and the drought stress mint tolerates poorly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hold steady soil moisture, mulch, hose the undersides repeatedly, conserve natural enemies, and shade the plants in extreme heat.

failure_diagnostics.label: Wilting stems that yellow and die back
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Verticillium wilt, a soil disease with no cure that shortens a mint patch's life.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Your mint grew slowly with a bronze cast in spring, then lower leaves yellowed and whole stems wilted and died, often on one side, in warm weather. That is verticillium wilt, a soilborne fungus with no cure. Next time, do not replant mint in that ground and do not plant it where tomatoes, potatoes, or strawberries grew; start fresh cuttings in clean soil somewhere else.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Remove infected plants, avoid replanting mint or following tomatoes and strawberries in that soil, and start clean cuttings in a new bed.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slow bronze-cast spring growth, one-sided branch development, and lower-leaf yellowing with warm-weather wilt and dieback indicate verticillium wilt (a soilborne Verticillium), which Utah State and the Connecticut Experiment Station flag for mint. The fungus persists in soil for years with a wide host range, so there is no rescue. Next time re-establish disease-free stock in clean ground away from prior Verticillium hosts and renew the patch on a multi-year cycle.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: A persistent soilborne Verticillium wilt, incurable and building up over years, worst after other host crops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rogue affected plants, propagate clean cuttings into clean ground away from tomato, potato, eggplant, and strawberry, and reset the patch periodically.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Mint is a perennial you plant once, not a succession crop. A single division or cutting establishes a permanent patch that regrows from its roots and rhizomes every spring and yields for years, so repeated sowings serve no purpose; the way to renew mint is to divide an overgrown clump or root fresh cuttings, not to re-sow. (Clemson HGIC; University of Minnesota; Utah State)

Set out a contained division or cutting in a pot or buried barrier in spring, around the last frost, in moist soil and part shade. It grows and gives leaves all through summer and into fall, then the top dies back after the first hard frost and it sleeps through winter as roots, coming back on its own each spring. Cut it back after frost knocks it down.
pnw.region_notes_seasoned: Mint is a very hardy herbaceous perennial and grows well throughout the maritime Pacific Northwest, though it is not the near-evergreen herb here that it is on the milder California coast: the region's real, if mild, winter still sends the top growth dormant. Set out a contained division, rooted cutting, or transplant around the last frost; it establishes through spring, is cut-and-come-again all summer, and the top dies back after the first hard fall frost while the crown and rhizomes overwinter. The immediate coast (z9) tends to run a later start but a longer, milder harvest tail into early winter than the valley interior (z8), reflecting the zone's milder extreme minimum temperature rather than a longer frost-free season. Shear the dead foliage at season's end, divide crowded clumps in early spring, and keep the planting contained: the runners spread aggressively in this region's moist soil.

description_seasoned: Mint (Mentha) is a hardy herbaceous perennial grown for its aromatic leaves, and it breaks nearly every rule the Mediterranean kitchen herbs follow. Where rosemary and thyme want lean, dry, sun-baked ground, mint wants rich, moist to damp soil and happily takes part shade, thriving in low, cool spots that defeat other herbs. It is very cold hardy (Utah State rates it to about -20°F, roughly USDA zones 3 to 9 and beyond), planted once from a division, cutting, or transplant and returning every spring from its roots. Its defining trait is aggression: mint spreads fast by underground rhizomes and above-ground stolons, and every extension source says the same thing, contain it in a sunken bottomless pot or a lined bed or it will take over. Spearmint (Mentha spicata) is the mild, sweet all-purpose culinary type; peppermint (Mentha x piperita) is the stronger, cooler, menthol one; and named mints, being hybrids and selections, come untrue from seed, so they are grown from cuttings and divisions. Harvest is cut-and-come-again all season, and frequent shearing keeps the leaves tender and heads off flowering.
description_beginner: Mint is one of the easiest herbs to grow, and it comes back every year on its own. Unlike most herbs, it loves moist soil and even grows in part shade, so it is happy in a cool, damp spot. The one thing to know about mint is that it spreads like crazy, running underground and popping up everywhere, so almost everyone grows it in a pot or a buried, bottomless container to keep it from taking over the garden. Grow it from a small plant or a cutting, not from seed, keep it watered, and snip sprigs whenever you want; the more you cut it, the better it grows. Spearmint is the mild, sweet everyday mint and peppermint is the stronger, cooler one, and there are fun flavors like chocolate and apple mint too.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Mint is ready to harvest once the plants are several inches tall and full, usually within weeks of establishing. Utah State picks when stems reach 3 to 4 inches and cuts two to three times a season, taking the stems to within about an inch of the soil; for everyday use, take sprigs or cut stems back by up to a third and the plant flushes again in a couple of weeks. Harvest in the cool morning for the best oils, and cut before or during flowering, since the leaves coarsen once it blooms.
harvest_ready_beginner: Mint is ready to pick once the plants are a few inches tall and leafy, which happens fast. Snip sprigs whenever you need them, or cut the whole plant back by a third and it grows again. Pick in the cool morning for the best flavor, and cut it before it flowers, since the leaves get tougher once it blooms.
